prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We observe a sharp transition from a singular, high-mass mode of star formation, to a low-mass dominated mode, in numerical simulations, at a metallicity of 10^-3 Zsolar. We incorporate a new method for including the radiative cooling from metals into adaptive mesh-refinement hydrodynamic simulations. Our results illustrate how metals, produced by the first stars, led to a transition from the high-mass star formation mode of Pop III stars, to the low-mass mode that dominates today. We ran hydrodynamic simulations with cosmological initial conditions in the standard LambdaCDM model, with metallicities, from zero to 10^-2 Zsolar, beginnning at redshift, z = 99. The simulations were run until a dense core forms at the center of a 5 x 10^5 Msolar dark matter halo, at z ~ 18. Analysis of the central 1 Msolar core reveals that the two simulations with the lowest metallicities, Z = 0 and 10^-4 Zsolar, contain one clump with 99% of the mass, while the two with metallicities, Z = 10^-3 and 10^-2 Zsolar, each contain two clumps that share most of the mass. The Z = 10^-3 Zsolar simulation also produced two low-mass proto-stellar objects with masses between 10^-2 and 10^-1 Msolar. Gas with Z >= 10^-3 Zsolar is able to cool to the temperature of the CMB, which sets a lower limit to the minimum fragmentation mass. This suggests that the second generation stars produced a spectrum of lower mass stars, but were still more massive on average than stars formed in the local universe.

outputs.L1:
We observe a sharp transition in numerical simulations from a singular, high-mass mode of star formation to a low-mass-dominated mode at a metallicity of \(10^{-3}\,Z_{\odot}\). We incorporate a new method for including radiative cooling from metals in adaptive mesh-refinement hydrodynamic simulations. Our results illustrate how metals produced by the first stars led to a transition from the high-mass star formation mode of Pop III stars to the low-mass mode that dominates today.

We ran hydrodynamic simulations with cosmological initial conditions in the standard \(\Lambda\)CDM model, with metallicities ranging from zero to \(10^{-2}\,Z_{\odot}\), beginning at redshift \(z = 99\). The simulations were run until a dense core formed at the center of a \(5 \times 10^{5}\,M_{\odot}\) dark matter halo at \(z \sim 18\). Analysis of the central \(1\,M_{\odot}\) core reveals that the two simulations with the lowest metallicities, \(Z = 0\) and \(10^{-4}\,Z_{\odot}\), contain one clump comprising 99% of the mass, whereas the two simulations with metallicities \(Z = 10^{-3}\) and \(10^{-2}\,Z_{\odot}\) each contain two clumps that share most of the mass. The \(Z = 10^{-3}\,Z_{\odot}\) simulation also produced two low-mass protostellar objects with masses between \(10^{-2}\) and \(10^{-1}\,M_{\odot}\).

Gas with \(Z \geq 10^{-3}\,Z_{\odot}\) can cool to the temperature of the CMB, which sets a lower limit on the minimum fragmentation mass. This suggests that second-generation stars produced a spectrum of lower-mass stars, though they remained more massive on average than stars formed in the local universe.
outputs.L2:
Numerical simulations show an abrupt change in star formation behavior at a metallicity of \(10^{-3} Z_{\odot}\), shifting from a single, massive-star formation mode to one dominated by lower-mass objects. To model this, we introduce a new technique for adding metal-line radiative cooling to adaptive mesh-refinement hydrodynamic simulations. The findings demonstrate that metals created by the first stars caused the transition from the massive Population III star formation mode to the lower-mass mode that is prevalent in the present-day universe.

We performed hydrodynamic simulations using cosmological initial conditions within the standard \(\Lambda\)CDM framework. The simulations began at redshift \(z = 99\) and covered metallicities ranging from zero to \(10^{-2} Z_{\odot}\). Each run was continued until a dense core developed at the center of a \(5 \times 10^{5} M_{\odot}\) dark matter halo, at approximately \(z \sim 18\).

An examination of the innermost \(1 M_{\odot}\) core shows that, in the two lowest-metallicity cases, \(Z = 0\) and \(10^{-4} Z_{\odot}\), nearly all the material—99% of the mass—resides in a single clump. By contrast, in the simulations with \(Z = 10^{-3}\) and \(10^{-2} Z_{\odot}\), the mass is mainly divided between two clumps. The \(Z = 10^{-3} Z_{\odot}\) run additionally formed two low-mass protostellar objects, with masses in the range \(10^{-2}\) to \(10^{-1} M_{\odot}\).

For gas enriched to \(Z \geq 10^{-3} Z_{\odot}\), cooling can proceed down to the cosmic microwave background temperature, which imposes a floor on the smallest fragmentation mass. These results indicate that second-generation stars likely formed with a distribution extending to lower masses, although their typical masses remained higher than those of stars forming in the nearby universe today.
outputs.L3:
Numerical simulations indicate a sharp transition in the character of star formation at a metallicity of approximately \(10^{-3} Z_{\odot}\), where \(Z_{\odot}\) denotes the metallicity of the Sun. Below this threshold, star formation remains dominated by the formation of a single massive object, while above it the gas fragments more efficiently, leading to the formation of multiple lower-mass clumps.

The study reaches this conclusion using a new method for incorporating radiative cooling by metals into adaptive mesh-refinement hydrodynamic simulations. This approach allows the simulations to follow the collapse of primordial and weakly enriched gas while accounting for the additional cooling channels provided by heavy elements. Since metal-line cooling can strongly affect the thermal evolution of collapsing gas, it plays a crucial role in determining whether the gas remains relatively warm and monolithic or cools enough to fragment.

In simulations with zero metallicity, \(Z = 0\), and very low metallicity, \(Z = 10^{-4} Z_{\odot}\), the collapse produces one dominant clump. This clump contains about 99% of the mass in the central core, indicating that fragmentation is inefficient under these conditions. Such behavior is consistent with the expectation that metal-free or extremely metal-poor gas forms very massive Population III stars, because the gas cannot cool effectively enough to break apart into many smaller fragments.

By contrast, simulations with metallicities of \(Z = 10^{-3} Z_{\odot}\) and \(Z = 10^{-2} Z_{\odot}\) show a markedly different outcome. In these cases, the central gas fragments into multiple clumps rather than collapsing into a single dominant object. The increased fragmentation suggests that metal cooling becomes efficient enough at these metallicities to lower the gas temperature, reduce the characteristic fragmentation mass, and promote the formation of lower-mass stars.

A key result is that gas with metallicity \(Z \geq 10^{-3} Z_{\odot}\) can cool down to the temperature of the cosmic microwave background. This temperature floor limits how cold the gas can become at high redshift, but it is still much lower than the temperatures typical of metal-free primordial collapse. As a result, second-generation stars formed from gas enriched above this critical metallicity were likely less massive than the first Population III stars. However, because the cosmic microwave background was warmer in the early universe than it is today, these second-generation stars were still expected to be more massive on average than stars forming in the present-day universe.
outputs.L4:
Numerical cosmological hydrodynamic simulations provide a powerful way to study how the first generations of stars formed in the early universe. In particular, they allow researchers to follow the collapse of primordial gas inside the first dark matter halos and to examine how small changes in gas composition alter the cooling, fragmentation, and eventual formation of protostellar clumps. A key question in early star formation is how the universe made the transition from Population III stars, which formed out of pristine hydrogen and helium gas and are thought to have been predominantly massive, to later generations of lower-mass stars that formed from gas enriched by the heavy elements produced in the first supernovae.

In this study, cosmological hydrodynamic simulations were carried out using a newly developed adaptive mesh-refinement technique that includes radiative cooling from metal lines. This method makes it possible to resolve the collapse of gas over a wide range of densities while accurately accounting for the additional cooling channels provided by elements heavier than helium. Because metals can radiate energy efficiently, even trace amounts of enrichment may strongly affect the thermal evolution of a collapsing cloud. The simulations therefore explored how different metallicities influence whether the gas remains relatively warm and forms massive objects, or cools more efficiently and fragments into smaller clumps.

The results show that metallicity has a decisive effect on the mode of star formation. In gas with extremely low or zero metallicity, cooling is inefficient and the collapse tends to produce a small number of massive protostellar objects, consistent with expectations for Population III star formation. However, once the metallicity reaches approximately \(10^{-3} Z_{\odot}\), where \(Z_{\odot}\) denotes the metallicity of the Sun, the behavior changes sharply. At this critical abundance, metal-line cooling lowers the gas temperature enough to promote fragmentation. Instead of collapsing into only one or a few massive clumps, the enriched gas breaks apart into multiple protostellar condensations with significantly lower characteristic masses.

This sharp transition suggests that enrichment by the first stars played a crucial role in changing the nature of star formation in the early universe. When massive Population III stars ended their lives as supernovae, they dispersed metals into their surroundings. Even a small amount of this enrichment could have allowed later gas clouds to cool more efficiently, fragment more readily, and form lower-mass second-generation stars. These stars would still have been more massive on average than stars forming in the present-day Milky Way, because the early universe remained warmer and less chemically evolved than modern star-forming regions. Nevertheless, the introduction of metals marked an important step toward the kind of low-mass dominated star formation that became common at later cosmic times.

Overall, the simulations demonstrate that the transition from primordial, high-mass star formation to metal-enriched, lower-mass star formation was not gradual but occurred near a well-defined critical metallicity of about \(10^{-3} Z_{\odot}\). This finding helps explain how the first heavy elements produced by Population III stars changed the thermal and dynamical properties of early gas clouds, enabling the formation of the first lower-mass stellar populations and shaping the subsequent evolution of galaxies.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for an astrophysics paper about simulations showing the critical metallicity for the transition from Population III high-mass star formation to low-mass star formation.
counterfactuals.output: We present a suite of three-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations investigating the transition from primordial, Population III star formation to the formation of low-mass stars in metal-enriched gas. By following the collapse and fragmentation of initially metal-free and weakly enriched minihalo gas over a range of metallicities, we identify a critical metallicity threshold above which efficient cooling alters the fragmentation scale and enables the formation of low-mass protostellar objects. Our results show that gas with metallicity below \(Z_{\rm crit}\) evolves similarly to primordial gas, remaining relatively warm and fragmenting only weakly, favoring the formation of massive Population III stars. In contrast, when the metallicity exceeds \(Z_{\rm crit}\), metal-line and dust-induced cooling reduce the gas temperature at high density, promote rapid fragmentation, and shift the characteristic stellar mass toward sub-solar and solar values. We find a critical metallicity of order \(Z_{\rm crit} \sim 10^{-5}-10^{-4}\,Z_\odot\), with the precise value depending on the assumed dust-to-metal ratio, depletion pattern, and thermodynamic history of the collapsing cloud. These simulations demonstrate that even trace enrichment by the first supernovae can strongly influence the stellar initial mass function and mark the onset of long-lived, low-mass star formation. Our findings provide a theoretical framework for interpreting the metallicity distribution of extremely metal-poor stars in the Galactic halo and for constraining the chemical feedback from the first generation of stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize numerical simulation results on how metal cooling affects fragmentation in early star-forming halos, including the metallicity threshold and redshift details.
counterfactuals.output:
Numerical simulations of early star-forming halos generally find that **metal cooling strongly increases fragmentation only after the gas metallicity exceeds a critical value**.

Key results:

- In **metal-free primordial gas**, cooling is dominated by H₂. The gas typically stalls at roughly  
  \[
  T \sim 200\ \mathrm{K}, \quad n \sim 10^4\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}},
  \]
  producing relatively large Jeans masses and favoring massive Pop III star formation with limited fragmentation.

- When trace metals are added, fine-structure cooling from species such as **C II and O I** can lower the gas temperature further, increasing fragmentation and producing smaller clumps.

- Simulations commonly find a critical metallicity of approximately  
  \[
  Z_{\rm crit} \sim 10^{-3.5} Z_\odot,
  \]
  or, in some calculations, a threshold bracketed between  
  \[
  Z \sim 10^{-4} Z_\odot \quad \text{and} \quad 10^{-3} Z_\odot .
  \]

- Below this threshold, e.g. at  
  \[
  Z \lesssim 10^{-4} Z_\odot,
  \]
  the thermal evolution remains close to the primordial case and fragmentation is weak.

- Above the threshold, e.g.  
  \[
  Z \gtrsim 10^{-3} Z_\odot,
  \]
  metal-line cooling becomes efficient, the gas reaches lower temperatures, and the collapsing cloud breaks into many more, lower-mass fragments.

- Redshift matters because the **cosmic microwave background sets a temperature floor**:
  \[
  T_{\rm CMB}=2.73(1+z)\ \mathrm{K}.
  \]
  Thus at:
  - \(z \sim 30\), \(T_{\rm CMB} \sim 85\) K,
  - \(z \sim 20\), \(T_{\rm CMB} \sim 57\) K,
  - \(z \sim 15\), \(T_{\rm CMB} \sim 44\) K.

  Even if metals cool the gas efficiently, the temperature cannot fall below this floor at high redshift, so fragmentation is enhanced but still limited by the CMB.

In summary, simulations show a transition from massive, Pop III-like star formation to more strongly fragmented, lower-mass star formation once the gas reaches roughly  
\[
Z_{\rm crit} \sim 10^{-3.5} Z_\odot,
\]
with the exact fragmentation scale depending on collapse redshift because the CMB temperature floor is higher at earlier times.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise research abstract describing AMR hydrodynamic simulations of primordial star formation with metallicities from zero to 10^-2 solar in a LambdaCDM cosmology.
counterfactuals.output: We present adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) hydrodynamic simulations of primordial star formation in a ΛCDM cosmological framework, following the collapse of gas in early minihaloes across metallicities from zero to \(10^{-2} Z_\odot\). The calculations resolve the thermal and dynamical evolution of star-forming gas over a broad density range, including non-equilibrium primordial chemistry, molecular cooling, and metal-line cooling where applicable. By varying the initial metallicity, we examine the transition from Population III to metal-enriched star formation and its impact on fragmentation, accretion structure, and characteristic collapse scales. Metal-free gas evolves quasi-self-similarly, with cooling dominated by H\(_2\) and high temperatures that favor massive central condensations. Even trace metal enrichment enhances cooling efficiency, lowers the gas temperature, and promotes fragmentation at higher densities, with increasingly complex filamentary and clumpy morphology toward \(10^{-2} Z_\odot\). Our results show that the thermal history set by metallicity strongly regulates the Jeans mass and fragmentation behavior in early haloes, suggesting a gradual rather than abrupt transition between primordial and low-metallicity star formation modes. These simulations provide a cosmological context for the emergence of the first metal-enriched stellar populations and constrain the environmental conditions governing the initial mass scale of early stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the main findings of a study where metal enrichment from the first stars causes gas in a 5 x 10^5 solar-mass dark matter halo at z ~ 18 to fragment into lower-mass protostars.
counterfactuals.output:
The study’s central result is that **metals produced by the first generation of stars can fundamentally change how gas collapses in early minihaloes**, shifting star formation away from the very massive, isolated Population III mode and toward **fragmentation into multiple lower-mass protostellar objects**.

Main findings:

- **Pristine gas forms massive stars:** In a metal-free halo, cooling is mainly by molecular hydrogen, which is inefficient below a few hundred kelvin. The gas stays relatively warm, the Jeans mass remains large, and collapse tends to produce one or a few massive Population III stars.

- **Metal enrichment boosts cooling:** When the gas in a roughly \(5 \times 10^5\,M_\odot\) dark-matter halo at \(z \sim 18\) is enriched by supernova ejecta from earlier first stars, elements such as carbon and oxygen provide additional radiative cooling through metal fine-structure lines. If dust is included, dust cooling can further enhance fragmentation at high densities.

- **Lower temperatures mean smaller fragments:** Because enriched gas can cool more efficiently, its characteristic Jeans mass decreases. Instead of collapsing monolithically into a massive object, the gas breaks apart into several dense clumps or protostellar cores.

- **Transition from Population III to Population II star formation:** The fragmentation suggests that even a small amount of metal pollution can mark the beginning of “normal” star formation, producing lower-mass Population II stars rather than exclusively massive primordial stars.

- **The resulting stars are still not necessarily like present-day stars:** At \(z \sim 18\), the cosmic microwave background temperature is about \(50\) K, which sets a temperature floor. So the typical fragment masses may remain higher than in modern molecular clouds, but they are much lower than expected for purely metal-free Population III collapse.

- **Metal distribution matters:** The study likely emphasizes that enrichment is inhomogeneous. Some regions remain pristine and continue forming massive Pop III stars, while enriched pockets fragment into lower-mass objects.

In short, the study shows that **the first supernovae can chemically “pre-condition” later minihaloes**, allowing gas to cool more effectively and fragment into smaller protostellar clumps. This provides a plausible pathway for the early Universe to transition from massive first-star formation to the more familiar, lower-mass mode of star formation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a scientific summary about the transition from Population III to second-generation star formation, emphasizing the role of a critical metallicity around 10^-3 Zsolar and CMB-limited cooling.
counterfactuals.output:
The transition from Population III (Pop III) to second-generation star formation marks a fundamental change in the thermal physics of early star-forming gas. Pop III stars formed from nearly metal-free primordial gas, where cooling was dominated mainly by molecular hydrogen. Because H₂ cooling becomes inefficient below temperatures of a few hundred kelvin, primordial gas generally fragmented weakly, favoring relatively massive stars compared with later stellar populations.

After the first supernovae enriched their surroundings with heavy elements, the cooling properties of collapsing gas changed. A key theoretical concept is a **critical metallicity**, often estimated to be around

\[
Z_{\rm crit} \sim 10^{-3} Z_\odot ,
\]

though the precise value depends on density, dust content, abundance pattern, radiation background, and dynamical history. Above this metallicity, metal fine-structure lines—especially from C and O—and, in some regimes, dust thermal emission can cool the gas more efficiently than H₂ alone. This enhanced cooling lowers the gas temperature and Jeans mass, promoting stronger fragmentation and enabling the formation of lower-mass, longer-lived second-generation stars.

However, at high redshift the gas cannot cool indefinitely. The **cosmic microwave background (CMB)** sets a temperature floor,

\[
T_{\rm CMB} = 2.73(1+z)\ {\rm K}.
\]

At redshifts \(z \sim 10–30\), this corresponds to tens of kelvin, comparable to or higher than the minimum temperatures reached in present-day molecular clouds. Even if metal cooling is efficient, the gas temperature cannot fall below this floor, and dust grains are also heated by the CMB. As a result, the minimum fragmentation mass in early enriched gas may remain higher than in the local Universe.

Thus, the Pop III to Pop II transition is controlled by the interplay between enrichment and thermal regulation. Metallicity near \(10^{-3} Z_\odot\) can allow gas to cool beyond the limits of primordial H₂ cooling, triggering a shift toward lower-mass star formation. Yet CMB-limited cooling at high redshift prevents the gas from reaching very low temperatures, potentially producing an early Population II initial mass function that is still somewhat top-heavy compared with that of present-day star formation. This transition therefore reflects not a sharp boundary, but a gradual change governed by metallicity, dust, redshift, and the local radiative and dynamical environment.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
